script.opening: (Friendly, sceptical, reasonable.) "The nurse said my blood pressure was up and I should see you about tablets. But honestly, it's only a bit high, isn't it? 142-ish. I feel completely fine. Do I really need to be on pills for the rest of my life at 58? Once you start them, that's it, isn't it — you're on them forever."

facts.text: "Home readings and the nurse's monitor. That was the average" — 7 days of home readings averaging 142/88. Clinic reading was 152/94.
"None of that. I feel fine" — no headaches, chest pain, breathlessness, visual problems or palpitations.

"Not that I know of. I've not had bloods for ages" — no diabetes, kidney problems, heart disease or stroke known. Dad had a heart attack at 66. Ex-smoker (stopped 10 years ago). BMI 28. Drinks about 18 units a week. Likes salty food — adds salt at the table.
"No, nothing regular." Occasional ibuprofen for his back. No allergies.
Office-based civil engineer. Walks the dog at weekends. Takeaways twice a week.
"I'm well. I don't want to be a patient. Once you're on pills, you're a patient." Wants "Proper reasons. Not just 'the number says so'."

Sceptical but open to evidence. If the doctor simply prescribes, push back politely. If the doctor explains risk-based decision-making: "So it might not need tablets at all?" and "And if it's high?" Appreciates fairness: "That's fairer than I expected." Will choose lifestyle changes: "Salt, probably. And more walking."

ice.ideas: "It's only a bit high and I feel fine — tablets would be for life."
ice.concerns: HIDDEN AGENDA — doesn't want to become "a patient"; wants control; his dad's heart attack is in the back of his mind.
ice.expectations: "Proper reasons" before any tablets — ideally to avoid them.

cues: "Once you're on pills, you're a patient." — what medication means to him.
"Proper reasons." — wants risk explained, not just the number.
Dad's heart attack — only if family history is asked.

checkpoints.text: CONFIRMS the diagnosis properly — clinic reading verified by ABPM or HBPM (NICE NG136 stage 1 = clinic 140/90–159/99 with ABPM/HBPM average 135/85–149/94) — rather than treating a single clinic reading, and recognises white-coat effect

Knows stage 1 treatment is a RISK-BASED decision — NICE NG136: discuss starting drugs (under 80) with target-organ damage, established CVD, renal disease, diabetes, or QRISK3 ≥10% (and consider if <60 even with lower 10-year risk), first-line calcium-channel blocker at 55 or over — NOT the BP number alone

Assesses the whole picture — estimates QRISK, checks for target-organ damage (urine ACR and haematuria dipstick, renal function/HbA1c/lipid bloods, ECG for LVH, fundi — arranged face to face), and considers secondary causes if features suggest
Emphasises LIFESTYLE (weight, salt, alcohol, exercise, diet, smoking, caffeine) for everyone, whether or not drugs start, as a meaningful BP/CVD-risk intervention

Reframes "tablets forever" honestly — treatment is reviewed at least annually and a dose reduction can be discussed if lifestyle lowers BP (clinical practice), though often long term; and where treatment is warranted, explains the genuine absolute benefits (stroke/MI/renal/eye protection)

Reads the reluctance (feeling well, anti-medicalisation, wanting control), respects his autonomy, and makes a genuine SHARED decision — neither dismissing the raised BP nor railroading him onto lifelong tablets
Explains risk and the decision in terms he can weigh, checks understanding, and supports an informed choice

Safety-nets and follows up: arranges the confirmatory/assessment tests, a monitoring/review plan whichever path is chosen, lifestyle support, when to reassess (and reconsider medication), and review of QRISK over time — a confirmed, risk-based, shared decision

worked.txt: "Good question, and I don’t want to put you on anything you don’t need. First, one raised reading isn’t a diagnosis — let’s make sure it’s genuinely up using home or 24-hour readings, not just the clinic, because some people’s rises only in here."

"Here’s the key thing: at this level, whether to treat isn’t about the number alone — it’s about your overall risk of heart attack and stroke over the next ten years. I’ll work that out with a score, check for any early effects on your heart and kidneys, and then we decide together."

"Let me estimate that risk — it uses your age, cholesterol, whether you smoke, family history and so on — and arrange a urine test, some bloods, a heart tracing and a look at the back of your eyes at the surgery. If those show your risk is low and there’s no damage, lifestyle alone may be reasonable. If they don’t, tablets genuinely protect you."

"Either way, the lifestyle stuff isn’t a fob-off — cutting salt and alcohol, losing a little weight, regular walking can drop your pressure meaningfully, sometimes enough to avoid or reduce tablets. That puts a lot back in your hands."

"And ‘on them for life’ isn’t automatic — we review every year, and if your lifestyle brings the pressure down we can talk about reducing the dose, though for many people it is long term. If you do need them, they’re quietly preventing a stroke years down the line, which is worth a lot even though you feel fine now."

"So nothing’s being forced today. Let’s get the readings and tests, I’ll show you your risk score, and we’ll make the call together. We’ll review it whatever we decide — this isn’t a one-way door. Does that feel fair?"

f.learning: A borderline blood-pressure decision is made in stages. First CONFIRM the diagnosis — do not treat a single clinic reading; verify with ambulatory (ABPM) or home (HBPM) monitoring, where (NICE NG136) stage 1 hypertension is a clinic BP of 140/90–159/99 with an ABPM/HBPM daytime average of 135/85–149/94, and stage 2 is clinic ≥160/100 and ABPM/HBPM ≥150/95 — which also excludes white-coat effect. Then recognise that in STAGE 1 the decision to start drug treatment is RISK-BASED, not number-based: NICE NG136 advises discussing starting antihypertensives with people under 80 with stage 1 hypertension who have target-organ damage, established cardiovascular disease, renal disease, diabetes, or a 10-year cardiovascular (QRISK3) risk ≥10%, and considering treatment in those under 60 with stage 1 even if the 10-year risk is <10% (10-year scores underestimate lifetime risk); first line at 55 or over is a calcium-channel blocker. So estimate QRISK and assess for target-organ damage (urine ACR and haematuria, renal function/HbA1c/lipids, ECG for LVH, fundi — the examination and ECG face to face), considering secondary causes if features suggest — the number alone does not decide it. Emphasise LIFESTYLE for everyone whether or not drugs start (weight, salt, alcohol, exercise, diet, smoking, caffeine), as it meaningfully lowers BP and CVD risk and can reduce or avoid medication. Reframe "tablets forever" honestly: treatment is reviewed at least annually and a dose reduction can be discussed if lifestyle lowers BP (clinical practice rather than an NG136 recommendation), though for many it is long term, and where warranted, explain the genuine absolute benefits (stroke, MI, renal and eye protection) the patient can weigh. The hidden agenda is feeling well, dislike of medicalisation and wanting control — respect autonomy, confirm the diagnosis, individualise with QRISK/organ-damage, offer lifestyle, and make a genuine SHARED decision, neither dismissing the raised BP nor railroading onto lifelong tablets, with monitoring and review whichever path is chosen.

knowledge.guideline: [1] NICE NG136 (hypertension in adults, updated November 2023) · [2] NICE NG238 (cardiovascular disease: risk assessment and reduction, 2023) · [3] DVLA Assessing fitness to drive (November 2025 edition)
knowledge.summary: An ABPM/HBPM average of about 142/88 is stage 1 hypertension. At 58, the drug decision rests on cardiovascular risk and target-organ damage, not the number alone — and NICE NG136 words it as a discussion, not an order. Lifestyle advice applies whatever he decides.

points.t: NICE NG136 [1]: offer ABPM (HBPM if ABPM unsuitable) when clinic BP is 140/90–180/120. Stage 1 = clinic 140/90–159/99 and ABPM/HBPM average 135/85–149/94. Stage 2 = clinic ≥160/100 and ABPM/HBPM ≥150/95. His average of about 142/88 is stage 1.

NICE NG136 [1]: urine ACR and dipstick for haematuria, HbA1c, U&E/eGFR, total and HDL cholesterol, fundi for hypertensive retinopathy, 12-lead ECG, and a formal cardiovascular risk estimate (QRISK3, NICE NG238 [2]).

NICE NG136 [1]: in people under 80 with stage 1 hypertension, discuss starting drug treatment if they have target-organ damage, established CVD, renal disease, diabetes, or a 10-year risk of 10% or more. Consider drug treatment under 60 with a 10-year risk below 10%, because 10-year scores underestimate lifetime risk. At 58 he falls in the ‘consider’ group even if his risk is low.

NICE NG136 [1]: aged 55 or over, or of Black African or African-Caribbean family origin — first-line calcium-channel blocker. Under 55 and not of that origin — ACE inhibitor or ARB. Target under 80: clinic below 140/90, ABPM/HBPM below 135/85. Doses per BNF.

NICE NG136 [1]: healthy diet and regular exercise, reduce salt, reduce alcohol if above recommended limits, discourage excessive caffeine, and stop smoking. Do not offer calcium, magnesium or potassium supplements to lower BP.
NICE NG238 [2]: if QRISK3 is 10% or more, offer atorvastatin 20 mg for primary prevention after lifestyle discussion. Share the number as an absolute risk.

Treatment is reviewed at least annually. If BP falls with lifestyle change, dose reduction can be discussed (clinical practice, not an NG136 recommendation). Be honest that for many people treatment is long term.

NICE NG136 [1]: clinic BP ≥180/120 with signs such as retinal haemorrhage or papilloedema, or life-threatening symptoms (new confusion, chest pain, heart failure, AKI), needs same-day specialist referral. DVLA [3]: Group 1 drivers need not notify for hypertension.

social.t: Feeling well and wanting to stay ‘not a patient’ is a common reason for declining treatment. Respect it and give him the facts to decide.

legal.t: Group 1 drivers need not notify for hypertension. Group 2 drivers are refused if resting BP is consistently ≥180 systolic or ≥100 diastolic (DVLA Assessing fitness to drive).

professional.t: GMC Decision making and consent (2020): explain options including no treatment, with benefits and risks in terms he can weigh. NICE NG197 (shared decision making, 2021) supports decision aids and absolute-risk communication.
NICE NG136 says ‘discuss starting’ for stage 1 with risk factors and ‘consider’ under 60 with low risk. Presenting it as mandatory misstates the guidance.

community.t: Blood Pressure UK and the British Heart Foundation for home-monitoring and salt reduction; community pharmacy BP checks.

playbook.diagnosis: Stage 1 hypertension confirmed on home/ambulatory average about 142/88 (NICE NG136). The drug decision depends on target-organ damage, CVD, renal disease, diabetes and QRISK3; at 58, treatment can be considered even if QRISK3 is below 10%.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Your pressure is mildly raised — not an emergency, but it adds to your chance of a stroke or heart attack over the years. Whether a tablet is worth it depends on your overall risk, which we can measure.”

management.reflectIce: “You want reasons, not orders — so let’s get your personal risk number and decide with it.”
management.psychosocial: Negotiate lifestyle he chooses (salt, walking). Keep him in charge of the decision.
sharedPlan: NG136 work-up: ACR, haematuria dip, HbA1c, U&E, lipids, fundi, ECG; QRISK3
Discuss or consider a CCB (first-line at 55+) depending on results; statin if QRISK3 ≥10% (NG238)
Lifestyle for all; annual review if treated
safetyNet: 999: sudden severe headache, visual change, chest pain, one-sided weakness

pitfalls.intro: This station rewards a correct NICE NG136 decision made with the patient, not for him. It is failed by prescribing on the number, by dismissing it, or by misquoting the thresholds.

items.fail: “142/88 needs treatment” — a prescription on the number alone.
items.why: In stage 1, NICE NG136 bases drug treatment on risk, organ damage and comorbidity.
items.fix: Plan the work-up and QRISK3, then discuss treatment with the result.

items.fail: “Your risk is under 10%, so no tablets.”
items.why: NG136 says consider drug treatment under 60 even with a 10-year risk below 10%.
items.fix: Explain that 10-year scores underestimate lifetime risk and offer the option.

items.why: NG136: CCB is first-line at 55 and over.
items.fix: Name the calcium-channel blocker if he chooses treatment.

items.fail: Lecturing on salt, alcohol and exercise.
items.why: A list of instructions earns little; a negotiated change scores.
items.fix: Ask which change is realistic for him and build on it.

items.fail: Promising tablets will be temporary, or that they are definitely for life.
items.why: False certainty damages trust when it proves wrong.
items.fix: Annual review, possible reduction if BP falls, honest that many continue long term.

items.fail: No teach-back and a vague ‘come back if worried’.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting is standard failing feedback.
items.fix: Name the 999 symptoms and book the results review.

wordPics.fail: Prescribes on the number alone, or dismisses stage 1 as ‘borderline, ignore it’; no QRISK or work-up; lectures about lifestyle; tells him tablets are definitely for life or definitely temporary.
wordPics.pass: Confirms stage 1 on home readings; plans the NG136 work-up and QRISK3; explains the risk-based decision; offers lifestyle advice; safety-nets.
wordPics.exc: All of that, plus: uses NICE NG136’s ‘discuss’ and ‘consider’ wording accurately (including the under-60 group); knows CCB is first-line at 58; negotiates the lifestyle change he chooses; is honest about ‘forever’; teach-back; he leaves feeling in charge.

avoid.dont: “Your blood pressure is high, so you need a tablet.”
avoid.instead: “At this level the decision depends on your overall risk. Let’s work that out and decide together.”
avoid.why: In stage 1, NICE NG136 bases the decision on risk, not the number.

avoid.instead: “It’s mild but real. Let’s find out what it means for you.”
avoid.why: Dismissal misses a treatable risk; he is in the ‘consider treatment’ group at 58.

avoid.dont: “Once you start, you’ll never come off them.”
avoid.instead: “We review every year; if your pressure falls we can talk about reducing.”
avoid.why: False certainty either way undermines trust.

NICE NG136 [1]: in people under 80 with stage 1 hypertension, discuss starting drug treatment if they have target-organ damage, established CVD, renal disease, diabetes, or a 10-year risk of 10% or more. Consider drug treatment under 60 with a 10-year risk below 10%, because 10-year scores underestimate lifetime risk. At 58 he falls in the ‘consider’ group even if his risk is low.

NICE NG136 [1]: aged 55 or over, or of Black African or African-Caribbean family origin — first-line calcium-channel blocker. Under 55 and not of that origin — ACE inhibitor or ARB. Target under 80: clinic below 140/90, ABPM/HBPM below 135/85. Doses per BNF.

NICE NG136 [1]: healthy diet and regular exercise, reduce salt, reduce alcohol if above recommended limits, discourage excessive caffeine, and stop smoking. Do not offer calcium, magnesium or potassium supplements to lower BP.
NICE NG238 [2]: if QRISK3 is 10% or more, offer atorvastatin 20 mg for primary prevention after lifestyle discussion. Share the number as an absolute risk.

Treatment is reviewed at least annually. If BP falls with lifestyle change, dose reduction can be discussed (clinical practice, not an NG136 recommendation). Be honest that for many people treatment is long term.

NICE NG136 [1]: clinic BP ≥180/120 with signs such as retinal haemorrhage or papilloedema, or life-threatening symptoms (new confusion, chest pain, heart failure, AKI), needs same-day specialist referral. DVLA [3]: Group 1 drivers need not notify for hypertension.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Open question first; let him state his objection to ‘pills forever’ in full.
Explored work and wellbeing, his wish to stay ‘not a patient’, lifestyle, over-the-counter drugs.
Picked up ‘only a bit up’ and ‘forever’; explored control and medicalisation.
Idea: numbers only slightly high. Concern: lifelong tablets, becoming a patient. Expectation: proper reasons.
Confirmed ABPM/HBPM; NG136 work-up (ACR, haematuria dip, HbA1c, U&E, lipids, fundi, ECG); QRISK3.
Primary vs secondary hypertension; white-coat effect excluded by home readings; target-organ damage.
Screened symptoms of accelerated hypertension and end-organ damage; knew the same-day criteria.
Stage 1 hypertension on ABPM/HBPM average 135/85–149/94; risk explained as a personal percentage.
NG136 stage 1 wording (discuss/consider); CCB first-line at 55+; lifestyle for all; statin if QRISK3 ≥10% (NG238).
Asked about drugs that raise BP; considered diabetes and CKD as treatment triggers.
Results review in 2–3 weeks; annual review if treated; teach-back; 999 symptoms named.

social.t: Feeling well and wanting to stay ‘not a patient’ is a common reason for declining treatment. Respect it and give him the facts to decide.

legal.t: Group 1 drivers need not notify for hypertension. Group 2 drivers are refused if resting BP is consistently ≥180 systolic or ≥100 diastolic (DVLA Assessing fitness to drive).

professional.t: GMC Decision making and consent (2020): explain options including no treatment, with benefits and risks in terms he can weigh. NICE NG197 (shared decision making, 2021) supports decision aids and absolute-risk communication.
NICE NG136 says ‘discuss starting’ for stage 1 with risk factors and ‘consider’ under 60 with low risk. Presenting it as mandatory misstates the guidance.

community.t: Blood Pressure UK and the British Heart Foundation for home-monitoring and salt reduction; community pharmacy BP checks.

redFlags: Severe headache, visual change, chest pain, breathlessness, confusion — accelerated hypertension
Clinic BP ≥180/120 with papilloedema or retinal haemorrhage — same-day referral
Clues to secondary hypertension (drugs, renal disease, endocrine features)
psychosocial: Feeling well; wanting to stay in control
Salt, alcohol, activity, weight — what he would change
ice: Idea: ‘only a bit up’, so treatment isn’t needed
Concern: lifelong tablets; becoming a patient
Expectation: proper reasons, not ‘the number says so’

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Stage 1 hypertension confirmed on home/ambulatory average about 142/88 (NICE NG136). The drug decision depends on target-organ damage, CVD, renal disease, diabetes and QRISK3; at 58, treatment can be considered even if QRISK3 is below 10%.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Your pressure is mildly raised — not an emergency, but it adds to your chance of a stroke or heart attack over the years. Whether a tablet is worth it depends on your overall risk, which we can measure.”

management.reflectIce: “You want reasons, not orders — so let’s get your personal risk number and decide with it.”
management.psychosocial: Negotiate lifestyle he chooses (salt, walking). Keep him in charge of the decision.
sharedPlan: NG136 work-up: ACR, haematuria dip, HbA1c, U&E, lipids, fundi, ECG; QRISK3
Discuss or consider a CCB (first-line at 55+) depending on results; statin if QRISK3 ≥10% (NG238)
Lifestyle for all; annual review if treated
safetyNet: 999: sudden severe headache, visual change, chest pain, one-sided weakness

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station rewards a correct NICE NG136 decision made with the patient, not for him. It is failed by prescribing on the number, by dismissing it, or by misquoting the thresholds.

items.fail: “142/88 needs treatment” — a prescription on the number alone.
items.why: In stage 1, NICE NG136 bases drug treatment on risk, organ damage and comorbidity.
items.fix: Plan the work-up and QRISK3, then discuss treatment with the result.

items.fail: “Your risk is under 10%, so no tablets.”
items.why: NG136 says consider drug treatment under 60 even with a 10-year risk below 10%.
items.fix: Explain that 10-year scores underestimate lifetime risk and offer the option.

items.why: NG136: CCB is first-line at 55 and over.
items.fix: Name the calcium-channel blocker if he chooses treatment.

items.fail: Lecturing on salt, alcohol and exercise.
items.why: A list of instructions earns little; a negotiated change scores.
items.fix: Ask which change is realistic for him and build on it.

items.fail: Promising tablets will be temporary, or that they are definitely for life.
items.why: False certainty damages trust when it proves wrong.
items.fix: Annual review, possible reduction if BP falls, honest that many continue long term.

items.fail: No teach-back and a vague ‘come back if worried’.
items.why: Non-specific safety-netting is standard failing feedback.
items.fix: Name the 999 symptoms and book the results review.
